text: The Keener's roasts
morning, over tea that was nearly black. His name was Tom
Garrity and he had known Edmund for forty years. "People
think he was lonely out here," he said. "He wasn't. He just
liked things written down. He said if nobody wrote it down,
it was as if the night hadn't happened."
"But who was it for?"
Garrity considered this. "There was a trawler went miss-
ing in 1973," he said. "The Marguerite, out of Peterhead. Six
men aboard. The inquiry wanted to know if she'd passed the
light, and when. Edmund had it: twenty past one in the
morning, heading east, lights showing. It didn't save any-
body. But the families knew how far she got." He put down
his cup. "After that I stopped asking who it was for."
She did not catch the Thursday train. She told herself it
was because of the weather, which was true as far as it went:
the wind had gone round to the north and the ferry was not
running. She spent the day carrying ledgers down to the
kitchen table, twelve at a time, and reading them in order.
Most nights were dull. A few were not. In February 1968
he had counted 43 vessels sheltering in the lee of the island
during a storm that lasted three days. In August 1979 he had
written, without comment, "Lights seen to the west at 02:10,
low on the water, not a ship." In the winter of 1985 there was
a gap of a single night, and beside it, in the margin, the
words "Influenza. Mrs. Garrity kept the count."
On Saturday the ferry ran again. Nora walked down to
the harbor, stood for some time looking at the timetable, and
then walked back up the hill. That evening, a little before
dusk, she found a pencil, opened the half-filled ledger to the
first empty page, and wrote the date at the top.
She did not know the proper way to describe the wind.
